title: Thank the courtier
hookLine: Seneca, flawed and rich, left the kindest letters

lines: A COACH WHO YELLED TOO MUCH.
NOT A PEDESTAL, NOT THE TRASH.
cards: A coach who changed your life and also yelled too much. A professor whose ideas you still use, and who turned out to have behaved badly. A parent who taught kindness and wasn't always kind.
Teachers like that are hard to put on a pedestal, and hard to throw away. Some readers put Seneca in exactly that spot. He wrote letters full of warmth and good sense.
He was also enormously rich, and he spent years at the side of Nero.

teach.b: First, the flaws, said plainly. Seneca was enormously wealthy, and ancient critics accused him of hypocrisy for preaching simplicity from his villas.

He was Nero's tutor, then his adviser, and stayed on through dark years; the historian Tacitus reports that after Nero had his own mother killed, Seneca was believed to have written the letter Nero sent the Senate explaining it away.
Earlier, exiled to Corsica, he wrote a consolation to a powerful official that reads, in places, like flattery aimed at winning his way home. Second, he knew.
Seneca imagines his critics asking why he talks one way and lives another.

teach.h: I'M NOT WISE, NOT EVEN CLOSE.
teach.b: He answers that he isn't wise, and isn't even close. He speaks about virtue, he says, not about himself, and when he criticizes faults, he includes his own. Third, the kindness.
The letters to Lucilius are full of it: the people who serve us are human beings like us; tears for a friend are allowed; begin now; trust a true friend as you trust yourself. Fourth, the end.
Accused of a part in a plot against Nero, Seneca was ordered to die. Tacitus tells us he asked for tablets to write his will and was refused.
So he turned to his friends and said that since he couldn't repay them, he would leave them the one thing he still had, and the finest: the pattern of his life.
Flawed and kind. Both true. You can thank him for the letters and still see the man clearly.

how: Some readers of Seneca hold both his wisdom and his compromises in view at once, valuing the letters while seeing the man clearly.

games.q: you're Seneca, ordered to die. you ask for tablets to write your will, and they're refused. what do you do?
o: tell your friends you leave them the pattern of your life
games.why: Tacitus says he turned to his friends and left them the one thing he still had, and the finest: the image of his life.

practice: Bring to mind one flawed teacher in your own life, a parent, a coach, a boss, a mentor, and let both sides come into view: what they gave you, and where they fell short or did harm.
If you're ready, let a small forgiveness loosen something, not saying it was fine, just setting down a little of the weight. If you're not ready, simply hold both sides honestly; that's enough today.

wordCard.voice: Tacitus, the Roman historian who reports that Seneca, rich and compromised at Nero's court, likely wrote the letter excusing a murder. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Tacitus Annals 15.62: the image or pattern of his life, Seneca's last bequest.

carryVoice: Your line: flawed and kind. Holding both is not the same as excusing either. Day six hundred ninety-one, done.
